title: CPI(M) and Unions Challenge IDBI Sale to Fairfax as Staff Set November Strike
excerpt: The ₹52,878-crore sale of 60.72% to Canada's Fairfax would be the largest foreign investment in an Indian bank; the government says employee terms and pensions are contractually protected.
body:
• The CPI(M) and bank unions have challenged the government's sale of a 60.72% stake in IDBI Bank to Canada's Fairfax Financial Holdings, flagging foreign ownership and valuation; IDBI staff strike nationwide on November 2-3.
  • The deal values the bank at about ₹52,878 crore: Fairfax offered ₹81 per share, above the ₹75.99 fair value set by two independent valuers.
  • DIPAM Secretary Arunish Chawla says the share purchase agreement bars any change to existing employees' service conditions to their disadvantage, and pension commitments are protected by a dedicated fund.
  • What this means for you: if you bank with IDBI, branches may be disrupted on November 2-3; the sale itself is not expected to complete until the end of the financial year, subject to RBI approval.

The government's landmark sale of IDBI Bank to a Canadian buyer has drawn a political and union challenge, with the CPI(M) raising foreign-ownership and valuation concerns and bank unions backing a two-day nationwide strike on November 2 and 3. The transaction — the largest foreign investment in an Indian bank — will see the government and LIC sell a combined 60.72 per cent stake to Fairfax Financial Holdings, led by Canadian billionaire Prem Watsa, for approximately ₹53,000 crore.

The deal on the table

The government's 30.48 per cent holding is valued at about ₹26,620 crore and LIC's 30.24 per cent at about ₹26,440 crore. Fairfax offered ₹81 per share, above the ₹75.99 benchmark fair value determined by two independent valuation agencies, according to PTI reporting. After the sale, the government and LIC intend to remain public shareholders capped at 15 per cent each, without board representation, and Fairfax will take responsibility for running the bank and meeting its future capital needs. Completion is expected by the end of the current financial year, subject to regulatory approvals including the Reserve Bank of India's.

The opposition case

The United Forum of Bank Unions, in a circular supporting the IDBI struggle, calls the sale "not only privatisation, rather it is foreignisation," pointing out that the bank holds about ₹3,50,000 crore in public deposits and has posted rising profits — ₹5,600 crore, ₹7,500 crore and ₹9,500 crore over the last three years, according to the UFBU circular. Unions also cite a December 2003 assurance in Parliament that the government would hold at least 51 per cent of IDBI, and the staff forum has demanded the government instead buy equity to restore a 51 per cent holding. The CPI(M) challenge echoes the same two themes: a profitable public institution passing to foreign control, and whether the price captures the bank's turnaround value.

"As per the share purchase agreement, the service conditions of the existing employees cannot be changed, modified or altered to their disadvantage by the strategic buyer."

— Arunish Chawla, Secretary, DIPAM

The government's answer

DIPAM Secretary Arunish Chawla told PTI that employees and pensioners have "nothing to fear": a dedicated pension fund has been set aside, all commitments will be honoured, and the bank will continue as a board-managed company under company and labour law, as it is today. He noted IDBI is not a nationalised bank, and its service conditions are set by its board in consultation with employees rather than by the government, according to PTI. The market regulator has separately directed LIC to trim its post-sale holding to 15 per cent, which would raise the bank's public float by four percentage points.

What happens next

The immediate test is the November 2-3 strike, called by the United Forum of IDBI Officers and Employees with UFBU solidarity programmes across the banking sector. The union forum also wants written statutory assurances on service conditions, pensions and reservation policies, plus an option for staff to transfer to public sector banks if the sale proceeds. None of that stops the transaction mechanically — the remaining gates are regulatory, led by the RBI — but a well-supported strike would raise the political cost of India's biggest bank privatisation weeks before it closes.
